quote: the essential forms and motifs of the world’s great mythologies—the “archaic forms” or “archetypes”—are collectively inherited in the individual psyche of each of us.
comment: Jung's claim, stated here as Wilber's setup before he complicates it: the starting point everyone (Freud, Jung, Piaget) agrees on before they split over what it means.

quote: It is not often realized that Freud was in complete agreement with Jung about the existence of this archaic heritage.
comment: The agreement Wilber wants readers to notice first — see people/freud.md and people/jung.md. Their fight (next annotation) is over interpretation, not over whether the archaic material exists.

quote: The question then centers—and here Freud and Jung bitterly parted ways—on the nature and function of these mythic motifs, these archetypes. Are they merely infantile and regressive (Freud), or do they also contain a rich source of spiritual wisdom (Jung)?
comment: The actual fault line. Wilber places himself close to Freud/Piaget on developmental origin while keeping some of Jung's respect for myth's value — see people/jung.md and people/piaget.md.

quote: Piaget, needless to say, sided with Freud on this particular issue.
comment: Piaget's stage sequence (magic → magic-mythic → concrete operational) is the empirical spine of this whole chapter — see people/piaget.md and concepts/holarchy.md.

quote: Campbell, we will see, believes that in certain circumstances (which we will explore), the early mythic archetypes can carry profound religious and spiritual meaning and power.
comment: Sets up the Campbell section a few pages later — the book's central worked example of the pre/trans fallacy. See people/campbell.md.

quote: “If there weren’t any words it would be very bad. You couldn’t make anything. How could things have been made?”
comment: One of Wilber's child-interview examples for magic-mythic cognition — the same egocentrism Piaget describes, not yet differentiated from the world.

quote: “No” is the first form of specifically mental transcendence.
comment: The pivot into the “Repression” section: language as the mechanism of the third fulcrum, differentiating mind from body — and, if it goes too far, dissociating them (repression, neurosis).

quote: our present-day worldwide ecological crisis is, in the very strictest sense of the term, a worldwide collective neurosis
comment: The chapter's payoff line — individual psychoneurosis (repressed biosphere) scaled up to civilizational ecological crisis. Worth its own concept page eventually.
